newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean strike leaders defy court order.
newsitem.headline: South Korean strike leaders defy court order.

text.p: Militant South Korean strike leaders huddled in the snow outside a Seoul cathedral defied an order to appear in court on Friday after riot police raided their headquarters during the night.
Police turned up at the red-brick Myongdong Cathedral soon after dawn to demand heads of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions appear before a Seoul judge.

State prosecutors have requested the court issue arrest warrants for confederation president Kwon Young-kil and six of his lieutentants for organising illegal strikes in protest at a new labour law that allows worker layoffs.
But a judge has said he wants to question the strike leaders first before issuing any arrest warrant, which would spark worker fury and bring fresh condemnation from international labour groups.
It was the second time plainclothes officers have approached Myongdong Cathedral bearing papers from the court, and once again they were rebuffed.
A gang of about 40 strikers guarding the union bosses blocked their entry to church grounds, which were blanketed in snow and ice.

"We will refuse any forceful detention," union representative Hwang Myung-jin told the officiers. "We are not staging illegal strikes. If we think it is necessary we will voluntarily appear and explain."
The sacred grounds of Myongdong Cathedral are a traditional refuge for militant workers, radical students and other opponents of the government.
Kwon and his deputies were holed up in a ramshackle plastic tent pitched in the shadow of the Roman Catholic cathedral with only two gas heaters to keep warm.

Shortly before midnight police investigators backed by several hundred riot police burst into the headquarters of the confederation and offices of its hospital and auto union affiliates, union officials said.
Anticipating the move, the union had earlier removed computers and floppy discs to a safe house.

The Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) asked the International Labour Organisation on Thursday to intervene immediately to prevent South Korea from arresting the seven strike leaders.
"We have also asked our member organisations to escalate pressure on South Korean representatives in their countries," spokesman Luc Demaret said.
He said the group had also decided to extend a mission to Seoul it has planned for later this week to protest against the new labour legislation. The team will now be in Seoul from January 11 to 16.
The ICFTU filed a complaint with the ILO in December against Korea's new law, saying it violated internationally recognised trade union rights.

It complained about provisions allowing strikers to be replaced by outside workers, banning dismissed workers from belonging to unions and barring companies from paying strikers during work stoppages.
Demaret said unions would stage protests against South Korea on Friday in various cities, including Brussels.
Kwon's outlawed confederation claims that around 200,000 of its 500,000 members are on strike, although the government puts the figure at less than half that number.

On Thursday the largest union body, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions with 1.2 million members, called on workers to join the biggest strike in South Korea's history for two days starting next Tuesday.
